title: What is Python 3.12's free-threaded (no-GIL) build and what changes?
description: PEP 703 free-threaded CPython, -X gil=0, and what it means for threading in 2025-26.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Python 3.13 ships an official free-threaded build (PEP 703, --disable-gil) where the GIL can be disabled so threads run truly in parallel on multiple cores; 3.12 introduced the groundwork behind a flag.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#1e40af"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#0e7490"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">GIL: 1 thread</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">No-GIL: N cores</text></svg>

| | GIL build (classic) | Free-threaded build (3.12+ experimental / 3.13 official) |
|---|---|---|
| Parallelism | 1 thread runs bytecode at a time | Many threads run bytecode in parallel |
| CPU-bound threads | No speedup, use multiprocessing | Real speedup, like Java/Go |
| Flag | default `python` | `PYTHON_GIL=0` / `python3.13t -X gil=0` |
| Cost | Simple memory model | Needs fine-grained locks, ~10% single-thread overhead |

CPython can now scale CPU-bound threads without multiprocessing — but you must handle thread-safety yourself and use atomic/thread-safe data or locks.

> **Interview tip:** Say 'PEP 703, free-threaded build, disable GIL with -X gil=0 / PYTHON_GIL=0, true parallelism for CPU-bound threads, but you now need real thread-safety' — then contrast with multiprocessing and C-extension GIL releases.

```python
import sys, threading
print(f"gil_enabled: {getattr(sys, '_is_gil_enabled', lambda: 'unknown')() if hasattr(sys, '_is_gil_enabled') else 'classic build'}")

# CPU-bound work now scales with threads on free-threaded build
import time, concurrent.futures
def crunch(n):
    return sum(i*i for i in range(n))
N = 2_000_000
start = time.perf_counter()
with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as ex:
    results = list(ex.map(crunch, [N]*4))
print(f"4 threads: {time.perf_counter()-start:.2f}s results[0]={results[0]}")
# On GIL build ~1x, on no-GIL build ~3-4x faster
```

title: When should you still use multiprocessing vs free-threaded threads in Python 3.12+?
description: Choosing threads vs processes now that GIL-free threading exists.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Even with no-GIL, multiprocessing still isolates memory/faults and avoids shared-state races; threads share memory and are lighter but require locks.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#7c3aed"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#059669"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Threads: shared mem</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Processes: isolated</text></svg>

| | Threads (no-GIL) | Multiprocessing |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | Shared — fast, but racy | Copy-on-write / pickle — safe |
| Scaling | Limited by contention on shared objects | Scales until IPC cost dominates |
| Crash isolation | One thread crash kills process | One process crash survives |
| Best for | CPU-bound NumPy-like loops, concurrent servers | CPU-bound with large isolated tasks, untrusted extensions |

Use threads for shared-memory parallelism where coordination is cheap; use processes for isolation, bypassing single-threaded C extensions, and true multi-interpreter safety.

> **Interview tip:** Default to threads for moderate CPU parallelism in 3.13t, but reach for multiprocessing when you need isolation, need to dodge non-thread-safe C extensions, or share little state.

```python
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor
import os
def work(x): return x*x

data = range(1000)
# Threads share memory - good for small coordinated tasks
with ThreadPoolExecutor() as ex:
    print("threads:", len(list(ex.map(work, data))))
# Processes isolate - good for heavy CPU batches
with ProcessPoolExecutor() as ex:
    print("processes:", len(list(ex.map(work, data))))
print(f"pid {os.getpid()} shows isolation")
```

title: How do you enforce match/case exhaustiveness in Python?
description: Exhaustive pattern matching with assert_never and static checkers.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Python's match has no runtime exhaustiveness; enforce it statically with `assert_never` (typing) + mypy/pyright --strict and a final `case _:` that raises.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#dc2626"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#16a34a"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Missing case = bug</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">assert_never = error</text></svg>

| | No check | With exhaustiveness |
|---|---|---|
| Code | `match x: case A: ... case B: ...` | `case _: assert_never(x)` |
| New variant added | Silent fallthrough | mypy/pyright error |
| Runtime | No error | Raises immediately if hit |
| Tool | none | mypy, pyright, pyrefly |

The checker flags any uncovered variant as `Never` mismatch, turning a missed case into a type error.

> **Interview tip:** Write `def assert_never(x: Never) -> Never: assert False` and end every match with `case _: assert_never(variant)` — then run pyright/mypy so a new union member forces a compile error.

```python
from typing import Never

def assert_never(x: Never) -> Never:
    raise AssertionError(f"Unhandled value: {x!r}")

from typing import Literal
Direction = Literal["north", "south", "east", "west"]

def move(d: Direction) -> None:
    match d:
        case "north": print("go north")
        case "south": print("go south")
        case "east": print("go east")
        case "west": print("go west")
        case _: assert_never(d)  # type checker errors if Direction grows

move("north")
# move("up")  # mypy/pyright: Argument not Literal
```

title: How does typing.Never enable exhaustive match checking?
description: Never as bottom type trick for pattern matching completeness.
answer:
**TL;DR:** `Never` is the bottom type (no values); if a match is exhaustive, the wildcard's variable narrows to `Never` and `assert_never` type-checks, otherwise it still has a variant and fails.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#4338ca"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#065f46"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Variant remains</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Narrows to Never</text></svg>

| | Type before assert_never | After exhaustive match | After non-exhaustive |
|---|---|---|
| Narrowed type | Union of remaining | `Never` (ok) | Still some variant (error) |
| Checker result | -- | Passes | `Arg of type X not assignable to Never` |
| Runtime | -- | No hit | Assertion fires |

`Never` makes the type checker prove you covered all cases — it's the same trick TypeScript uses with `never` in switch exhaustiveness.

> **Interview tip:** Explain Never = uninhabited type; last case `_` should be unreachable, so `assert_never` only type-checks when exhaustive — demo with `Literal` union and missing branch error.

```python
from typing import Never, Union
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Circle: r: float
@dataclass
class Square: s: float
Shape = Union[Circle, Square]

def area(shape: Shape) -> float:
    match shape:
        case Circle(r=r): return 3.14*r*r
        case Square(s=s): return s*s
        case _: assert_never(shape)

print(area(Circle(2)))
print(area(Square(3)))
# Add @dataclass class Triangle -> pyright errors until you add case Triangle
```

title: What is asyncio.TaskGroup and why does it replace gather?
description: Structured concurrency in Python 3.11+ with TaskGroup.
answer:
**TL;DR:** `asyncio.TaskGroup` (3.11) provides structured concurrency: tasks are scoped to the `async with` block, auto-cancelled on error, and errors combine into an `ExceptionGroup`.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#be123c"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#0f766e"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">gather: loose</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">TaskGroup: structured</text></svg>

| | asyncio.gather | asyncio.TaskGroup |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Unscoped, manual cancel | Scoped `async with` auto-joins/cancels |
| Error on multi-fail | First exception (or return_exceptions) | `ExceptionGroup` with all errors |
| Cancellation | Must cancel children yourself | Cancels siblings on first error |
| Readability | Loose | Structured, like `with` for concurrency |

TaskGroup guarantees no leaked tasks and explicit cancellation semantics — `gather` can leave dangling tasks if you don't cancel manually.

> **Interview tip:** Prefer `async with TaskGroup() as tg: tg.create_task(...)` for any fan-out; only use `gather` for simple 2-3 awaits or when you need `return_exceptions=True` legacy behavior.

```python
import asyncio

async def fetch(n, fail=False):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1*n)
    if fail: raise ValueError(f"fail {n}")
    return n*10

async def demo():
    # Structured: all tasks finish or all cancel together
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tg.create_task(fetch(1))
            tg.create_task(fetch(2, fail=True))
            tg.create_task(fetch(3))
    except* ValueError as eg:  # ExceptionGroup handler
        print(f"caught {len(eg.exceptions)} error(s):", eg.exceptions)

asyncio.run(demo())
```

title: How does TaskGroup handle cancellation and ExceptionGroup?
description: Sibling cancellation and except* interaction with TaskGroup.
answer:
**TL;DR:** On any child failure, TaskGroup cancels remaining siblings and waits for them, then raises a single ExceptionGroup aggregating all child exceptions.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#9f1239"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#115e59"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">1 fail -> cancel rest</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">+ ExceptionGroup</text></svg>

| | Task fails | Sibling tasks | Parent after block |
|---|---|---|
| TaskGroup | Exception stored | Cancelled via asyncio.CancelledError | Raises ExceptionGroup |
| gather | Exception stored | Keeps running unless cancelled | Raises first exception |
| Timeout | Use `asyncio.timeout` inside | Auto-cancel | Raises TimeoutError + group |

This mimics structured concurrency in Kotlin/Go: the parent scope owns child lifetimes, so no task outlives its group.

> **Interview tip:** Mention `except*` is required to handle ExceptionGroup, and `asyncio.timeout(2)` inside TaskGroup gives deadline-aware structured concurrency.

```python
import asyncio

async def worker(n, delay):
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(delay)
        return n
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print(f"worker {n} cancelled")
        raise

async def main():
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tg.create_task(worker(1, 0.5))
            tg.create_task(worker(2, 0.1))
            # This fails fast and cancels worker 1
            async def failing():
                await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
                raise RuntimeError("boom")
            tg.create_task(failing())
    except* RuntimeError as eg:
        print("group failed:", eg.exceptions)

asyncio.run(main())
```

title: How does Pydantic v2 validation work (BaseModel, field_validator, mode)?
description: Pydantic v2 patterns trending in 2025-26 FastAPI codebases.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Pydantic v2 validates via Rust core (pydantic-core), with `mode='before'/'after'`, `Annotated` types, and `field_validator`/`model_validator`.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#7e22ce"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#15803d"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Raw JSON -></text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Validated model</text></svg>

| | Pydantic v1 | Pydantic v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Core | Python | Rust (pydantic-core) |
| Validator | `@validator` | `@field_validator`, `@model_validator` |
| Parse | `parse_obj` / `parse_raw` | `model_validate` / `model_validate_json` |
| Config | `class Config` | `model_config = ConfigDict(...)` |
| Speed | Baseline | 5-50x faster |

V2 is 5-50x faster than v1 and uses `model_validate` / `model_dump` instead of `parse_obj` / `dict`.

> **Interview tip:** Show `Annotated[str, StringConstraints(min_length=3)]` and `field_validator('email', mode='before')` + `model_config = ConfigDict(str_strip_whitespace=True)` as the 2025 idiom.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator, ConfigDict, ValidationError
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import StringConstraints

class User(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(str_strip_whitespace=True)
    name: Annotated[str, StringConstraints(min_length=2)]
    age: int
    email: str

    @field_validator('age')
    @classmethod
    def check_age(cls, v):
        if v < 0 or v > 150: raise ValueError('age out of range')
        return v

print(User.model_validate({"name": " Ada ", "age": 30, "email": "a@b.com"}))
try:
    User.model_validate({"name": "A", "age": 200, "email": "bad"})
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e.errors()[0]['type'])
```

title: How do TypeAdapter, strict mode, and computed fields work in Pydantic v2?
description: Beyond BaseModel: validating arbitrary types and derived fields.
answer:
**TL;DR:** `TypeAdapter` validates any type without a model, `strict=True` forbids coercion, and `@computed_field` exposes derived properties in serialization.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#6d28d9"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#047857"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">TypeAdapter(any)</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">@computed_field</text></svg>

| | Feature | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| TypeAdapter[List[int]] | Validate bare types, JSON columns | No model needed |
| `strict=True` | Reject `'123'` for `int` | API boundary hardening |
| `@computed_field` | Derived `full_name` from `first+last` | Include in `model_dump` |
| `mode='wrap'` | Custom parsing + call next | Sanitization |

These cover the 80% of Pydantic use outside models — query params, JSON columns, and API response shaping.

> **Interview tip:** Demo `TypeAdapter[list[int]].validate_json('[1,2,3]')` and `strict=True` rejecting string ints — interviewers love asking why loose coercion is dangerous at API edges.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, TypeAdapter, computed_field
from typing import List

adapter = TypeAdapter[List[int]]
print(adapter.validate_json('[1, 2, 3]'))
strict_adapter = TypeAdapter[int](config={"strict": True})
try:
    strict_adapter.validate_python("123")
except Exception as e:
    print("strict rejected:", type(e).__name__)

class Rect(BaseModel):
    w: float
    h: float
    @computed_field
    @property
    def area(self) -> float:
        return self.w * self.h

print(Rect(w=3,h=4).model_dump())  # includes area
```

title: Polars vs pandas: when should you switch in 2025-26?
description: Performance, lazy execution, and interop trade-offs.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Polars is a Rust-based DataFrame with lazy query planning and true parallelism; pandas is NumPy-based eager. Polars wins on large data, pandas wins on ecosystem maturity.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#991b1b"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#1d4ed8"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">pandas: eager</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Polars: lazy+parallel</text></svg>

| | pandas | Polars |
|---|---|---|
| Engine | NumPy/Python, single-threaded | Rust, multi-threaded |
| Execution | Eager | Lazy (query optimizer) + eager |
| Memory | Copies often | Zero-copy Arrow, streaming |
| API | Mature, huge ecosystem | Faster, smaller but growing |
| Interop | Direct | `to_pandas()` / `from_pandas()` |

For new services handling >1M rows, Polars + lazy gives 5-30x speedup; keep pandas where your stack is Spark/pandas-native.

> **Interview tip:** Say 'Polars for speed and scale, pandas for ecosystem' and show `pl.scan_parquet(...).filter(...).collect()` lazy example vs pandas eager.

```python
import polars as pl
import pandas as pd

# Polars lazy pipeline (optimizer fuses filter+projection)
# df = pl.scan_parquet("data.parquet").filter(pl.col("age")>30).select(["name","age"]).collect()
# Demo with in-memory:
df_pl = pl.DataFrame({"name":["Ada","Bob","Cara"], "age":[31,25,40]})
print(df_pl.filter(pl.col("age")>30))

# pandas eager equivalent
df_pd = pd.DataFrame({"name":["Ada","Bob","Cara"], "age":[31,25,40]})
print(df_pd[df_pd["age"]>30])

# Zero-copy interop
print("to_pandas:", type(df_pl.to_pandas()))
```

title: How does Polars LazyFrame query optimization work?
description: Predicate pushdown, projection pushdown, and streaming.
answer:
**TL;DR:** LazyFrame builds a logical plan; `collect()` optimizes it (predicate/projection pushdown, CSE) then executes in parallel streaming batches.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#3b0764"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#064e3b"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Plan -> Optimize -></text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Parallel Execute</text></svg>

| | Eager DataFrame | LazyFrame |
|---|---|---|
| When executed | Immediately per op | Only on `collect()` |
| Optimization | None | Pushdown, pruning, parallel |
| Parquet scan | Reads all | Reads only used columns/rows |
| Memory | Full materialization | Streaming, bounded |

This is why scanning Parquet lazily reads only needed columns/rows, like a database query planner.

> **Interview tip:** Explain `scan_parquet -> filter -> select -> collect` chain and that `.explain()` prints the optimized plan — great live-demo.

```python
import polars as pl
lf = pl.LazyFrame({"a":[1,2,3,4], "b":[10,20,30,40], "c":["x","y","z","w"]})
q = lf.filter(pl.col("a")>2).select(["a","b"])
print(q.explain())  # shows optimized plan
print(q.collect())
# Streaming for larger-than-RAM:
# pl.scan_parquet("big.parquet").filter(pl.col("a")>2).collect(streaming=True)
```

title: What is uv and why is it replacing pip/poetry in 2025-26?
description: Astral's Rust package manager — 10-100x faster.
answer:
**TL;DR:** `uv` is Astral's Rust-based drop-in for pip/pip-tools/virtualenv/poetry; it resolves and installs 10-100x faster with a global cache and `uv.lock`.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#7c2d12"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#1e3a8a"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">pip: slow Python</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">uv: fast Rust</text></svg>

| | pip + venv | poetry | uv |
|---|---|---|
| Speed | Baseline | ~2x pip | 10-100x pip (Rust) |
| Resolver | pip legacy | poetry solver | Rust PubGrub |
| Lockfile | requirements.txt | poetry.lock | uv.lock |
| Python mgmt | pyenv/conda | poetry env | `uv python pin` |
| Install cmd | `pip install -r req.txt` | `poetry install` | `uv sync` |

Single binary `uv` handles `venv`, `pip install`, `run`, `tool`, and `lock` — no more `pip` + `venv` + `poetry` juggling.

> **Interview tip:** Know `uv venv`, `uv pip install`, `uv sync`, `uv run script.py`, `uv tool install ruff`, and that `uv.lock` + `pyproject.toml` replaces requirements.txt.

```python
# pyproject.toml (uv)
# [project]
# name = "myapp"
# dependencies = ["fastapi>=0.110", "polars"]
# [tool.uv]
# python = "3.12"

# Shell (not Python) workflow:
# uv venv --python 3.12
# uv sync              # install from uv.lock
# uv add "pydantic>=2" # add dep + relock
# uv run python app.py # run in project env
# uv tool install ruff # install global tool isolated
print("uv sync is 10-100x faster than pip install -r requirements.txt")
```

title: How do uv workspaces and named dependency groups work?
description: Monorepo with uv's Cargo-like workspaces.
answer:
**TL;DR:** `uv` workspaces (like Cargo) let one `uv.lock` manage multiple packages; `[dependency-groups]` and `tool.uv.sources` wire local path deps.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#451a03"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#312e81"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Single uv.lock</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Many packages</text></svg>

| | Without workspaces | With workspaces |
|---|---|---|
| Lockfiles | One per package, drift | One root `uv.lock` |
| Local dep | `pip install -e ../lib` | `tool.uv.sources = {lib = {workspace=true}}` |
| Sync | Per package | `uv sync` at root builds all |
| Groups | `optional-dependencies` | `[dependency-groups] dev = [...]` |

This replaces `poetry` monorepo hacks and `pip -e` editable installs with a single `uv sync` at the root.

> **Interview tip:** Show `[tool.uv.workspace] members = ["packages/*"]` + `members` + `uv sync` and `dependency-groups` for dev/test — the 2025 monorepo answer.

```python
# Root pyproject.toml
# [tool.uv.workspace]
# members = ["packages/api", "packages/lib"]
#
# [dependency-groups]
# dev = ["pytest", "ruff"]
#
# packages/api/pyproject.toml
# [project]
# dependencies = ["mylib"]
# [tool.uv.sources]
# mylib = { workspace = true }

# Commands:
# uv sync --group dev   # install with dev group
# uv run --package api pytest
print("workspace: single lock, many packages")
```

title: How do Unpack and TypedDict enable type-safe **kwargs?
description: PEP 692 Unpack for kwargs typing in 2025-26 APIs.
answer:
**TL;DR:** `Unpack[TypedDict]` (3.11, PEP 692) types `**kwargs` as a struct: each kwarg name and type is checked, with `Required`/`NotRequired`.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#581c87"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#064e3b"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">**kwargs: Any</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Unpack[TD]: strict</text></svg>

| | Plain **kwargs | Unpack[TypedDict] |
|---|---|---|
| Type | `**kwargs: Any` (unchecked) | `**P: Unpack[MyKwargs]` (checked) |
| Misspelled kw | No error | Type error |
| IDE autocomplete | None | Full kwarg hints |
| Use | Legacy | New 3.11+ APIs |

This finally makes wrapper/decorator `**kwargs` forwarding type-safe without `**kwargs: Any`.

> **Interview tip:** Show `class Kw(TypedDict, total=False): ...` + `def f(**kw: Unpack[Kw])` and that `Required` marks must-pass kwargs — the decorator wrapper pattern.

```python
from typing import TypedDict, Required, NotRequired, Unpack

class MovieKwargs(TypedDict, total=False):
    title: Required[str]
    year: int
    director: NotRequired[str]

def create_movie(**kw: Unpack[MovieKwargs]) -> str:
    return f"{kw['title']} ({kw.get('year','?')})"

print(create_movie(title="Dune", year=2021))
# create_movie(year=2021)  # error: missing Required title
# create_movie(title="X", unknown=1)  # error: extra kw

# Forwarding preserves types:
def wrapper(**kw: Unpack[MovieKwargs]):
    return create_movie(**kw)
print(wrapper(title="Inception", director="Nolan"))
```

title: What is TypeVarTuple and Unpack for variadic generics?
description: PEP 646 variadic generics — typing heterogeneous tuples/arrays.
answer:
**TL;DR:** `TypeVarTuple` (PEP 646, 3.11) lets a generic capture an arbitrary tuple of types: `tuple[*Ts]`; `Unpack` spreads it.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#4c1d95"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#022c22"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Generic[T] one type</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">Generic[*Ts] many</text></svg>

| | TypeVar | TypeVarTuple |
|---|---|---|
| Arity | One type | Variable length tuple of types |
| Syntax | `Generic[T]` | `Generic[*Ts]` where `Ts = TypeVarTuple('Ts')` |
| Example | `list[T]` | `tuple[*Ts]`, `Array[*Shape]` |
| Unpack | `Unpack[TypedDict]` | `*Ts` in `tuple[*Ts]` |

It types `Array[*Shape]`, `Callable` with precise args, and typed `zip`/`map` over heterogeneous data.

> **Interview tip:** Example is `def move(*args: *Ts) -> tuple[*Ts]` or `NDArray[*Shape]` pattern — mention `*Ts` star syntax and `Generic[*Ts]`.

```python
from typing import Generic, TypeVarTuple, Unpack

Ts = TypeVarTuple('Ts')

class Array(Generic[Unpack[Ts]]):
    def __init__(self, *dims: Unpack[Ts]): self.dims = dims
    def shape(self) -> tuple[Unpack[Ts]]: return self.dims

# Heterogeneous typed tuple
def first_two(a: tuple[Unpack[Ts]]) -> tuple[Unpack[Ts]]:
    return a

arr = Array(3, 4, 5)
print(arr.shape())  # (3, 4, 5)
print(first_two((1, "hi", 3.14)))
```

title: What is except* and ExceptionGroup in Python 3.11+?
description: PEP 654 — handling multiple unrelated exceptions together.
answer:
**TL;DR:** `ExceptionGroup` bundles multiple exceptions (from TaskGroup or manual `raise ExceptionGroup`); `except*` matches and extracts compatible sub-exceptions, leaving the rest.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#7f1d1d"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#1e1b4b"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">except: first only</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">except*: all matching</text></svg>

| | except | except* |
|---|---|---|
| Matches | First matching exception | All matching sub-exceptions |
| With ExceptionGroup | Catches group as one | Unwraps and handles per type |
| Multiple types | Need nested try | `except* A` + `except* B` chain |
| Introduced | Always | 3.11 (PEP 654) |

It's the missing piece for structured concurrency where N tasks fail with N different errors at once.

> **Interview tip:** Contrast `except ValueError` vs `except* ValueError as eg:` and show `eg.exceptions` plus splitting: handled vs unhandled subgroups.

```python
try:
    raise ExceptionGroup("two fails", [ValueError("bad value"), TypeError("bad type"), ValueError("again")])
except* ValueError as eg:
    print(f"caught {len(eg.exceptions)} ValueError(s)")
    for e in eg.exceptions: print(" -", e)
except* TypeError as eg:
    print(f"caught {len(eg.exceptions)} TypeError(s)")

# Non-matching stays unhandled -> would propagate
# With TaskGroup, except* is the only way to handle partial failures
```

title: How do you raise and split ExceptionGroups manually?
description: Constructing, catching, and splitting exception groups outside asyncio.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Raise with `ExceptionGroup(msg, excs)` or `BaseExceptionGroup`; split with `eg.split(Type)` into (matched, rest) or `except*` sugar.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#881337"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#1e293b"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">One raise, many errors</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">split / except*</text></svg>

| | Method | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `raise ExceptionGroup` | Bundle many | One raise carries all |
| `except* T` | Handle T subgroup | Non-T auto re-raised |
| `eg.split(T)` | `(matched, rest)` tuple | Manual handling |
| `eg.subgroup(T)` | Only matched | Filter view |

Use `eg.split()` when you need to handle some and re-raise the rest programmatically.

> **Interview tip:** Show `matched, rest = eg.split(ValueError)` and that `except*` is syntax sugar for split+re-raise.

```python
try:
    raise ExceptionGroup("batch", [ValueError("v1"), RuntimeError("r1"), ValueError("v2")])
except ExceptionGroup as eg:
    matched, rest = eg.split(ValueError)
    if matched:
        print(f"handled {len(matched.exceptions)} ValueErrors")
    if rest:
        print(f"unhandled {len(rest.exceptions)} left")
        # raise rest  # re-raise remainder

# except* equivalent (cleaner):
try:
    raise ExceptionGroup("batch2", [ValueError("a"), TypeError("b")])
except* ValueError as eg:
    print("except* ValueError:", eg.exceptions)
except* TypeError as eg:
    print("except* TypeError:", eg.exceptions)
```

title: How do you read TOML with tomllib in Python 3.11+?
description: stdlib TOML parsing for pyproject.toml without third-party deps.
answer:
**TL;DR:** `tomllib` (3.11, PEP 680) parses TOML from binary files via `tomllib.load(f)`; it is read-only — write with `tomli-w` if needed.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#5b21b6"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#0c4a6e"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">tomllib: stdlib read</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">tomli-w: write</text></svg>

| | tomllib (stdlib) | tomli / tomli-w | toml (legacy) |
|---|---|---|
| Read | `tomllib.load(fb)` | `tomli.load(fb)` | `toml.load(f)` |
| Write | Not supported | `tomli_w.dump(obj, fb)` | `toml.dump(obj, f)` |
| Mode | Binary `rb` | Binary | Text |
| Since | 3.11 | Backport for <3.11 | Pre-PEP 680 |

Perfect for reading `pyproject.toml` / `uv.lock` metadata without adding `tomli` dependency.

> **Interview tip:** Remember `open('pyproject.toml','rb')` binary mode and that `tomllib` returns dict; for writing, add `tomli-w` or use `tomllib`+manual for now.

```python
import tomllib
from pathlib import Path

# Write a sample TOML to parse (normally you'd read pyproject.toml)
sample = b'[project]\nname = "myapp"\nversion = "1.2.3"\nrequires-python = ">=3.11"\n'
# From bytes:
data = tomllib.loads(sample.decode())
print(data["project"]["name"])

# From file (binary mode!):
# with open("pyproject.toml", "rb") as f:
#     cfg = tomllib.load(f)
#     print(cfg["project"]["dependencies"])

# Conditional import for <3.11 compat:
try:
    import tomllib
    print("tomllib available")
except ImportError:
    import tomli as tomllib  # backport
    print("using tomli backport")
```

title: How do pyproject.toml, tomllib, and uv/pyproject workflows fit together?
description: Modern Python packaging metadata in 2025-26.
answer:
**TL;DR:** `pyproject.toml` (PEP 621) is the single project file; `tomllib` reads it stdlib, `uv`/`pip` consume `[project]` and `[tool.*]` tables.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#6b21a8"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#155e75"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">pyproject.toml</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">tool.uv + [project]</text></svg>

| | Old layout | New (PEP 621) |
|---|---|---|
| Metadata | setup.py / setup.cfg | `[project]` in pyproject.toml |
| Deps | requirements.txt | `[project.dependencies]` + `uv.lock` |
| Tool config | many dotfiles | `[tool.*]` sections |
| Read in code | `tomli` | `tomllib` (3.11+) |
| Build | `setup.py` | `pyproject.toml` + hatch/pdm/uv |

`[project]` holds portable metadata; `[tool.ruff]`, `[tool.uv]`, `[tool.pytest]` hold tool config — one file replaces setup.cfg/setup.py/requirements.

> **Interview tip:** Show reading `cfg['project']['dependencies']` and that `uv add` edits pyproject.toml and relocks — the 2025 packaging answer.

```python
import tomllib
toml_text = b'''
[project]
name = "demo"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = ["fastapi","pydantic>=2"]
[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100
'''
cfg = tomllib.loads(toml_text.decode())
print("name:", cfg["project"]["name"])
print("deps:", cfg["project"]["dependencies"])
print("ruff:", cfg["tool"]["ruff"])
# uv workflow: uv add fastapi -> edits [project.dependencies] and updates uv.lock
```

title: What is Python 3.12's new type parameter syntax (type, generic classes)?
description: PEP 695 — `type`, `class Foo[T]`, and `def f[T]()` replacing TypeVar boilerplate.
answer:
**TL;DR:** PEP 695 (3.12) adds `type Alias[T] = ...`, `def f[T](x: T) -> T`, and `class Stack[T]:` — inline type params without `TypeVar` declarations.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="640" height="120" role="img"><rect width="640" height="120" rx="12" fill="#0f172a"/><rect x="20" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#1e1b4b"/><rect x="340" y="20" width="280" height="80" rx="10" fill="#3f6212"/><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">TypeVar = TypeVar('T')</text><text x="480" y="65" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="monospace" font-size="14">def f[T](x: T)</text></svg>

| | Pre-3.12 | 3.12+ (PEP 695) |
|---|---|---|
| Func generic | `T = TypeVar('T'); def f(x: T) -> T` | `def f[T](x: T) -> T` |
| Class generic | `class C(Generic[T]):` | `class C[T]:` |
| Type alias | `Alias: TypeAlias = list[int]` | `type Alias[T] = list[T]` |
| Scope | Module global | Lexically scoped to def/class |

Old `TypeVar` still works but new syntax is cleaner and scoped; `type` creates proper generic type aliases.

> **Interview tip:** Mention `type Vector[T] = list[T]` and `class Stack[T]:` plus that `T` is scoped inside brackets — no more `TypeVar` at module top.

```python
from typing import reveal_type

# 3.12+ syntax (also works via `from __future__ import annotations` on 3.11 with pyright)
# def first[T](xs: list[T]) -> T:
#     return xs[0]
# class Stack[T]:
#     def __init__(self): self._d: list[T] = []
#     def push(self, v: T): self._d.append(v)
#     def pop(self) -> T: return self._d.pop()
# type IntStack = Stack[int]

# Portable fallback that type-checkers understand today:
from typing import TypeVar, Generic
T = TypeVar('T')
def first(xs: list[T]) -> T: return xs[0]
class Stack(Generic[T]):
    def __init__(self): self._d: list[T] = []
    def push(self, v: T): self._d.append(v)
    def pop(self) -> T: return self._d.pop()

s: Stack[int] = Stack()
s.push(42)
print(first([1,2,3]), s.pop())
print("PEP 695 on 3.12: def f[T](x: T) -> T and class C[T]:")
```
